candidates.name: Publicly Break the Specific Thing Customers Hate About the Whole Category
candidates.mechanism: In a commoditized category, every competitor tends to share the same customer-unfriendly norms (contracts, fees, fine print) because none of them wants to be the first to give up the revenue those norms generate. Publicly and permanently eliminating one of those specific, named pain points — not vaguely promising 'better service' — gives customers a concrete, easy-to-repeat reason to switch that has nothing to do with price.
candidates.evidence: T-Mobile's 'Un-carrier' campaign, launched March 2013, eliminated specific industry-standard practices (annual contracts, overage fees) rather than simply cutting prices. Per T-Mobile's own investor press releases, the company led the U.S. wireless industry in postpaid phone net customer additions for multiple consecutive quarters following the launch, reporting 643,000 branded postpaid phone net additions in Q3 2013 alone and continued momentum through Q4.
candidates.transferTemplate: Instead of competing on 'we're the best HVAC company in town' (a claim every competitor also makes), identify the one specific practice customers in the category quietly hate — vague arrival windows, no upfront pricing, no-show techs — and publicly commit to eliminating it, by name. A concrete, named commitment is something a customer can repeat to a neighbor; a vague quality claim isn't.

candidates.name: Use a Distinct Voice the Whole Category Is Too Cautious to Use
candidates.mechanism: When every competitor in a boring, commoditized category markets the same way (clinical, feature-focused, interchangeable), a genuinely different voice — sharp, funny, willing to say what customers actually think — stands out precisely because the category has trained customers to expect sameness. The product itself doesn't have to be different for the voice to be.
candidates.evidence: Dollar Shave Club's March 2012 launch video — an irreverent, comedic ad that cost roughly $4,500 to produce — drove the company's site to crash from traffic within 90 minutes of posting and brought in 12,000 subscribers in the first 48 hours and 25,000 within the first week, entering a razor market long dominated by Gillette's conventional, feature-focused advertising. The story is independently reported by multiple outlets including Inc. magazine.
candidates.transferTemplate: Every competitor's website and ads in a commoditized local trade tend to read identically (a stock photo of a smiling worker, generic promises of quality and reliability). A genuinely distinct voice — in a review response, a truck wrap, a local ad, a service reminder text — doesn't require a different service to stand out; it just requires being willing to sound like an actual person instead of the category's default tone.

candidates.name: Make Direct Price Comparison Impossible by Being the Only Source
candidates.mechanism: A commodity gets shopped on price precisely because it's identical everywhere it's sold. Offering something structurally unique — not just branded differently, but genuinely unavailable anywhere else — removes the customer's ability to comparison-shop at all, because there's nothing to compare it against.
candidates.evidence: Per retail-industry trade publication Supermarket News, roughly 80% of Trader Joe's product offerings are private label, versus roughly 25% at a typical grocery competitor. Industry analysts quoted in the piece attribute this directly to Trader Joe's deliberately selling items (like its 'Unexpected Cheddar' or 'Cookie Butter') that customers cannot find at any other retailer, eliminating price-comparison shopping for those products entirely rather than competing through promotional discounting.
candidates.transferTemplate: In categories where the actual service is genuinely interchangeable (mowing a lawn, spraying for pests), the way out of price comparison is to attach something to the job that a competitor doesn't offer at all — a proprietary product mix, a specific guarantee structure, a bundled service nobody else in the area bundles — something a customer literally cannot get quoted elsewhere, not just a version of the same thing done slightly better.
